title: How to Register Your Address in Japan
summary: After moving to Japan or moving within Japan, you may need to register your address at your city or ward office. This is one of the first important steps for daily life.
keywords: How to Register Your Address in Japan | Japan Life Explained 🐾 Japan Life Explained Articles About FAQ Official resources Sources Disclaimer City Office & ID How to Register Your Address in Japan After moving to Japan or moving within Japan, you may need to register your address at your city or ward office. This is one of the first important steps for daily life. Quick answer Address registration connects your legal address to your Residence Card and local municipality. It can affect health insurance, resident tax, My Number, bank accounts, phone contracts, and official mail. Go to the city or ward office that handles your new address and complete the required moving procedure. Simple diagram Move to a new address new home in Japan → City / ward office submit moving notice → Address is recorded Residence Card and records Why address registration matters Your registered address is used for many everyday systems in Japan. If your address is not registered or is outdated, other procedures may become difficult. Moving within the same city or ward You may need to submit a moving notice for the new address within the same municipality. Moving to another city or ward You may need procedures at both the old and new municipalities, such as moving-out and moving-in notices. Leaving Japan You may need to notify the municipality before leaving, especially if ending your residence in Japan. Typical moving procedures Moving in Submit a moving-in notice at the city or ward office for your new address. Moving out If moving to another municipality, you may need a moving-out procedure at your old office. Address change If moving within the same municipality, the procedure may be called an address change or moving within the city. Residence Card update The new address may be written or updated on your Residence Card. title: The Bank & Phone Loop in Japan
summary: In Japan, opening a bank account and getting a mobile phone number can feel like a loop. A bank may ask for a phone number, while a phone company may ask for a bank account or Japanese payment method.
keywords: The Bank & Phone Loop in Japan | Japan Life Explained 🐾 Japan Life Explained Articles About FAQ Official resources Sources Disclaimer Daily life The Bank & Phone Loop in Japan In Japan, opening a bank account and getting a mobile phone number can feel like a loop. A bank may ask for a phone number, while a phone company may ask for a bank account or Japanese payment method. Quick answer The loop happens because banks, phone companies, and payment services all want a way to confirm your identity, contact you, and collect payment. The easiest way out is usually to prepare your Residence Card, registered address, contact method, and payment option before applying. Simple diagram Bank account may ask for phone number → Phone contract may ask for bank account or card → Payment setup may need both This is why people sometimes feel stuck: each service asks for something from another service. Why this happens For many services in Japan, companies need to know where you live, how to contact you, and how you will pay. If one of those pieces is missing, the application may become harder. Banks may want a Japanese phone number so they can contact you or verify your application. Mobile phone companies may want a bank account, credit card, or payment method. Online services may ask for SMS verification, which requires a usable phone number. Some applications may be harder if your address is not registered yet. A practical order that may help 1. Register your address Go to your city or ward office after moving in and register your address on your Residence Card. 2. Prepare a contact method If possible, use a temporary phone plan, prepaid SIM, eSIM, or contact number accepted by the service. 3. Try a bank that accepts your situation Some banks are easier for new residents, students, or employees than others. 4. Set up phone payment Once you have a bank account or accepted card, phone contracts and online services become easier. title: How to Visit a Clinic in Japan
summary: Visiting a clinic in Japan is usually organized and practical, but the reception process, insurance check, and prescription system can feel confusing the first time.
keywords: How to Visit a Clinic in Japan | Japan Life Explained 🐾 Japan Life Explained Articles About FAQ Official resources Sources Disclaimer Health & Insurance How to Visit a Clinic in Japan Visiting a clinic in Japan is usually organized and practical, but the reception process, insurance check, and prescription system can feel confusing the first time. Quick answer When visiting a clinic in Japan, bring your health insurance proof, Residence Card, cash or payment method, and any medication information. At reception, you may fill out a medical questionnaire, wait, see the doctor, pay at the counter, and then take your prescription to a pharmacy. Simple diagram Reception show insurance proof → Questionnaire symptoms and history → Doctor visit examination → Payment & prescription clinic then pharmacy Before you go Many clinics accept walk-ins, but some require reservations. It is safer to check the clinic website or call first if you can. Some clinics have specific hours for first-time patients. Check the department For example: internal medicine, dermatology, ophthalmology, dentistry, orthopedics, or ENT. Check clinic hours Many clinics close during lunch and may have different hours by day. Bring documents Insurance proof, Residence Card, and medication information are useful. Prepare simple symptom words Writing symptoms on your phone can help if Japanese is difficult. What to bring Health insurance card, My Number health insurance card, or eligibility document Residence Card Cash or payment method Medication notebook, if you have one List or photo of medicines you currently take Referral letter, if another doctor gave you one Your address and phone number At reception At the clinic reception desk, staff usually check your insurance information and ask whether it is your first visit. You may receive a medical questionnaire called 問診票 . The questionnaire may ask about your symptoms, allergies, current medicines, medical history, pregnancy status, and emergency contact. After seeing the doctor After the examination, you usually return to the waiting area and wait for payment. If medicine is needed, the clinic may give you a prescription. In many cases, you take the prescription to a pharmacy nearby. 🐱 Cat tip: In Japan, the clinic and pharmacy are often separate. Do not be surprised if you pay at the clinic and then pay again at the pharmacy. title: Guarantor Companies in Japan: What Renters Should Know
summary: When renting an apartment in Japan, you may be asked to use a guarantor company. This can be confusing because it feels like another fee on top of rent, deposit, and key money.
keywords: Guarantor Companies in Japan: What Renters Should Know | Japan Life Explained 🐾 Japan Life Explained About FAQ Articles Official resources Request a topic Disclaimer Housing Guarantor Companies in Japan: What Renters Should Know When renting an apartment in Japan, you may be asked to use a guarantor company. This can be confusing because it feels like another fee on top of rent, deposit, and key money. Quick answer A guarantor company is a company that helps guarantee rent payment to the landlord. Many rental contracts in Japan require one, even if you have a job or enough savings. The tenant usually pays a guarantor fee at the start and may also pay renewal fees. Simple diagram Tenant rents the apartment → Guarantor company guarantees payment → Landlord reduces payment risk Why guarantor companies are used Landlords want confidence that rent will be paid. In the past, many contracts required a personal guarantor, often a family member. Now many properties use guarantor companies instead. For foreign renters, this can be especially common because landlords may worry about language, visa status, length of stay, overseas emergency contacts, or whether rent can be collected if there is a problem. What the fee usually means The guarantor fee is not rent and is usually not a deposit. It is a fee paid to the guarantor company for providing the guarantee service. The fee structure depends on the company and property. Initial guarantor fee A fee paid when signing the contract. It may be based on rent or a fixed amount. Renewal fee Some guarantor companies charge a renewal fee every year or at contract renewal. Monthly fee Some contracts include a monthly guarantor or payment service fee. Late payment cost If rent is late, extra fees or collection procedures may apply. Check the contract carefully. title: Health Insurance in Japan: What New Residents Should Know
summary: Japan has public health insurance systems. If you live in Japan, you usually need to be enrolled in a health insurance system and show your insurance card or eligibility confirmation when visiting a clinic.
keywords: Health Insurance in Japan: What New Residents Should Know | Japan Life Explained 🐾 Japan Life Explained Articles About FAQ Official resources Sources Disclaimer Health & Insurance Health Insurance in Japan: What New Residents Should Know Japan has public health insurance systems. If you live in Japan, you usually need to be enrolled in a health insurance system and show your insurance card or eligibility confirmation when visiting a clinic. Quick answer Health insurance in Japan usually reduces the amount you pay at clinics and hospitals. Many working employees are covered through their employer. People who are not covered by employer insurance usually join National Health Insurance through their city or ward office. Simple diagram You live in Japan resident status and address → Join insurance employer or city office → Visit clinic show insurance proof Two common types Employee health insurance Many full-time employees and some part-time employees are enrolled through their employer. The insurance premium is usually deducted from salary. National Health Insurance People not covered by employee insurance often enroll at the city or ward office. Premiums are usually paid to the municipality. What insurance usually does When you use public health insurance at a covered clinic or hospital, you usually pay only part of the medical cost at the counter. The exact share can depend on age, income, and situation. Health insurance does not mean everything is free. You still usually pay a portion of the cost, and some services may not be covered. Insurance card, My Number card, and eligibility Japan is changing how people show health insurance eligibility. Some people use a My Number card registered for health insurance, while others may use other confirmation documents depending on their situation. 🐱 Cat tip: When visiting a clinic, bring your Residence Card and any health insurance proof you have, especially if you are not sure what the clinic accepts. title: How to Read a Japanese Payslip

Start by separating it into earnings, deductions, and final payment. Quick answer To read a Japanese payslip, first find the total earnings, then find the total deductions, and finally find the amount actually paid. The final payment may be written as 差引支給額 or another similar term depending on the company system. Simple diagram 支給 earnings / payments − 控除 deductions ＝ 差引支給額 final paid amount The three main areas 1. Earnings area This shows salary, overtime pay, commuting allowance, and other payments. 2. Common earnings items Basic salary Your regular base salary before overtime or extra allowances. Overtime pay Additional pay for overtime work, if applicable. Commuting allowance Money paid for commuting costs. It may appear as a separate item. Other allowances Depending on the company, there may be housing, family, qualification, or position allowances. Common deduction items 所得税 Income tax withheld from your salary. 住民税 Resident tax. It may start later depending on your situation. 健康保険 Health insurance deduction. 厚生年金 Employees' pension insurance deduction. 雇用保険 Employment insurance deduction. その他控除 Other deductions, such as company-specific fees, if applicable. title: Resident Tax in Japan: Bills and Payslip Deductions
summary: Received a resident tax bill, or noticed a new deduction on your payslip? This guide explains what the tax is, why it may appear later, and how payment works. If you have moved, check which municipality handles your bill.
keywords: Resident Tax in Japan: Bills and Payslip Deductions | Japan Life Explained 🐾 Japan Life Explained Articles About FAQ Official resources Sources Disclaimer Salary & Tax Resident Tax in Japan: Bills and Payslip Deductions Received a resident tax bill, or noticed a new deduction on your payslip? This guide explains what the tax is, why it may appear later, and how payment works. If you have moved, check which municipality handles your bill. Quick answer Resident tax is a local tax, separate from national income tax. It is usually based on the previous calendar year’s income. As a rule, the municipality where you live on 1 January assesses it. Payment may be through salary deductions or bills you pay yourself. Exemptions and personal circumstances matter, so income does not always mean tax is due. Moving later in the year does not simply cancel the bill. Check your own municipality for billing details. Simple diagram Last year’s income basis for calculation → Municipality calculates city/ward/town/village → This year’s payments salary deduction or bills Why it feels delayed Resident tax often does not feel like an immediate tax. That is because the tax amount is usually calculated after the year ends, based on income information from the previous year. This creates a timing gap: Year 1 You earn income in Japan. After Year 1 Your income information is reported and processed. Year 2 Resident tax based on Year 1 income may start being collected. How resident tax is paid Special collection Your employer deducts resident tax from your salary and pays it to the municipality. This is common for employees. Ordinary collection You receive tax bills from the municipality and pay them yourself. This may happen in some situations. The method can depend on your employment status, timing, and municipality procedures. Why your take-home pay may drop If resident tax was not deducted during your first months or first year, your take-home pay may feel higher at first. Later, when resident tax starts, your monthly take-home pay may become lower even if your gross salary did not change. 🐱 Cat tip: A lower second-year take-home pay does not always mean your salary went down. Resident tax may have started. title: Why Is My Take-home Pay Lower Than My Salary in Japan?
summary: Your salary offer or contract usually shows gross salary. The money that arrives in your bank account is take-home pay after taxes and social insurance deductions.
keywords: Why Is My Take-home Pay Lower Than My Salary in Japan? | Japan Life Explained 🐾 Japan Life Explained Articles About FAQ Official resources Sources Disclaimer Salary & Tax Why Is My Take-home Pay Lower Than My Salary in Japan? Your salary offer or contract usually shows gross salary. The money that arrives in your bank account is take-home pay after taxes and social insurance deductions. Quick answer In Japan, your monthly salary usually has several deductions before you receive it. Common deductions include income tax, resident tax, health insurance, pension, employment insurance, and sometimes company-specific items. Your bank transfer amount is the final amount after those deductions. Simple diagram Gross salary amount before deductions → Taxes & insurance deducted from salary → Take-home pay amount paid to you The basic idea When people first work in Japan, the most surprising thing is often that the salary amount written in the contract is not the amount paid into the bank account. This is normal. The contract amount is usually gross salary , and the transfer amount is net pay or take-home pay . Think of your salary in three layers: 1. Earnings Base salary, overtime pay, commuting allowance, and other payments. 2. Deductions Taxes, social insurance, pension, and other amounts subtracted. 3. Final payment The amount actually transferred to your bank account. Common deductions Income tax A national tax withheld from your salary. The amount depends on income and other conditions. Resident tax A local tax paid to your municipality. It often starts later, so it can surprise people in their second year. Health insurance Insurance that helps reduce medical costs when you visit clinics or hospitals. Pension Public pension contribution. It is often one of the larger monthly deductions. Employment insurance A smaller deduction related to unemployment and employment support programs. Company-specific items Some companies may deduct cafeteria fees, union fees, housing, or other items if applicable. Why resident tax surprises people Resident tax is often based on your income from the previous year. Because of that, some new workers may not see much resident tax at first, but it may appear later. This timing is one of the most common surprises for foreign residents and new employees. 🐱 Cat tip: If your second-year take-home pay suddenly feels lower, resident tax may be one reason. title: I lost my job: what to do first
summary: A first checklist after you leave a job: employer documents, Hello Work, unemployment benefits, insurance, pension and tax.
keywords: Quick answer Start with three things: your last day of employment, your insurance end date, and the papers your employer will provide. Contact Hello Work about job support and possible unemployment benefits. Check health insurance and pension procedures separately. Do not wait for a benefit decision before checking these procedures. Tax bills and residence procedures may also need attention. This guide is a starting checklist for people whose job has ended. It also helps if your contract ended or you chose to leave. First: write down the dates Make a short note with: Your last day of employment. The date your employer's health insurance ends. Your next job's start date, if you have one. The date the next employer expects your insurance to start. Your final working day and your last day of employment may differ. Ask your employer if you are unsure. A new job offer does not, by itself, tell you when insurance begins. Keep letters from your employer and public offices together. Note who you contacted and what you still need. You do not need to understand every system before asking for help. Ask your employer for the right papers These papers serve different purposes. Ask when and how you will receive each one that you need. Paper What it helps you do Employment separation documents, 離職票 Ask Hello Work about unemployment benefits. Check both the employment details and the stated reason for leaving. A document showing your employment insurance number Help Hello Work find your insurance record. Proof that workplace health insurance has ended, 資格喪失証明書 Show the end of your previous coverage when arranging new insurance. Ask the receiving office which proof it accepts. Salary withholding statement, 給与所得の源泉徴収票 Keep a record of salary and income tax. You may need it for your next employer or tax procedures. Final payslip Check the final payment and deductions. For an employee leaving during the year, the employer's deadline to issue the salary withholding statement is within one month after leaving. Ask the employer first if it does not arrive. The National Tax Agency provides guidance for missing statements. For the final payslip, see How to read your payslip . Contact Hello Work Hello Work is Japan's public employment service. Ask the office serving your address about job-search support and employment insurance benefits. The basic allowance, 基本手当, is a benefit for eligible jobseekers. Leaving a job does not automatically start payments. Hello Work checks your insurance history, reason for leaving, and ability and intention to work. The usual insurance-history requirement is at least 12 qualifying months in the two years before leaving. Certain reasons for leaving may allow a different rule: at least six months in the previous year. Hello Work decides which rule applies to your case. Tell Hello Work if you cannot start work now because of illness, pregnancy, or another reason. Ask which procedure applies instead of assuming you can claim the usual benefit immediately. If your separation documents have not arrived, ask your employer and contact Hello Work. If the stated reason for leaving is wrong, explain the problem to Hello Work. Do not assume you must accept an incorrect reason. Before visiting, check the office's current document list. You may need your separation documents, identity and My Number documents, and details of a bank account in your name. Ask about language support when arranging the visit; availability varies. Check deadlines without confusing them with payment dates Unemployment benefits have a waiting period and may have a further restriction period. These do not mean money will reach your account on a promised date. The seven-day waiting period is part of the benefit procedure. It does not simply start on your last day at work. For resignations on or after April 1, 2025, the usual restriction for leaving without a justifiable reason is one month. Exceptions apply. Ask Hello Work about your own timetable, including any relevant training rules. Health insurance and pension procedures have separate deadlines. Check those now, even while your benefit application is being considered. Arrange health insurance and check your pension For health insurance, start by asking who will cover you after your workplace coverage ends. A new employer, your previous insurer, your municipality, or a family member's insurer may be the right contact. The companion guide Health insurance after leaving a job explains the options and the deadlines to check. For the basic systems, read Health insurance in Japan . For pension coverage, ask whether your next job will include Employees' Pension Insurance. If there is a gap, another registration procedure may be needed. The companion guide Pension when your work situation changes explains the routes and payment-difficulty support. Health insurance and pension are separate checks. Completing one procedure does not prove that the other is complete. Keep tax and residence notices on your checklist Leaving work does not mean a resident-tax bill disappears. Ask your former employer or municipality how any remaining tax will be collected. Keep payment notices and check their dates. See Resident tax for the previous-income explanation. Depending on your status of residence, you may need to notify the Immigration Services Agency. Check the official guidance for your status. Your employer's reporting and your own procedures are not necessarily the same. Also check the expiry date on your residence card. This guide does not decide whether a new job fits your status of residence. Ask Immigration Services Agency staff when you are unsure. If you are moving, Address registration covers a separate procedure. Where to ask Former employer: employment dates, missing papers, final pay and deductions. Hello Work: job search, benefit eligibility, missing separation papers and disputed leaving reasons. Health insurer or municipality: your next health coverage. Municipal pension counter or pension office: pension registration and payment difficulties. Immigration Services Agency: procedures linked to your status of residence. Useful words Japanese English meaning When you may use it 離職票 Employment separation documents When asking your employer for papers for Hello Work. 雇用保険 Employment insurance When checking your insurance history. 基本手当 Basic unemployment allowance When asking Hello Work about possible benefits. 資格喪失 Loss of insurance eligibility When confirming when old coverage ends. 源泉徴収票 Withholding statement When asking for your salary and tax record. Related guides Continue with the companion guides Health insurance after leaving a job and Pension when your work situation changes . Use the linked payslip, health-insurance, resident-tax and address guides above for background. Official sources Hello Work: employment insurance procedures — documents and application steps. Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare: unemployment benefit questions — eligibility and current payment restrictions. National Tax Agency: missing salary withholding statements . Immigration Services Agency: notifications about affiliated organisations . Some sources are in Japanese. Use the named office if the guidance does not answer your situation.

title: Health insurance after leaving a job
summary: Compare health insurance routes after leaving a job, including a new employer, voluntary continuation, National Health Insurance and family coverage.
keywords: Quick answer Ask when your current health coverage ends and when any new coverage begins. Then check four possible routes: a new employer, voluntary continuation, National Health Insurance, or a family member's workplace insurance. Eligibility and cost vary. Contact the relevant insurer or municipality promptly. Do not choose only by comparing the deduction on your old payslip. First: check the coverage dates Ask your former employer for the date you lose eligibility for its health insurance. Ask for a document confirming that date. If you have another job, ask the new employer whether you will be enrolled and when coverage starts. A gap between jobs may require another arrangement. Do not keep using your former workplace's insurance after your eligibility ends. Having a card or document does not mean the old coverage is still valid. If you need medical care during a change, ask your insurer how to confirm your current eligibility. For background on the systems and proof of coverage, see Health insurance in Japan . Compare the four routes These are possible routes, not four options that everyone can freely choose. Route Who to contact First question New employer's health insurance The new employer's HR or payroll team Will I be enrolled, and from which date? Voluntary continuation of previous insurance The insurer you belonged to before leaving Am I eligible, and what is the application deadline? National Health Insurance The municipality where you live Do I need to enrol, and what documents and cost estimate are available? Coverage as a family dependant The family member's employer or health insurer Could I qualify, and when would coverage start? If you are covered by a different system because of age or another condition, ask your municipality which procedure applies. This guide does not cover every special arrangement. Route 1: a new employer's health insurance Ask the new employer to confirm enrolment. Do not use the job's start date as a substitute for the insurance start date. Useful questions include: Will this job include workplace health insurance? What is the start date of my coverage? What proof can I use before the insurance information is updated? Which papers do you need from me? If you have already joined National Health Insurance, ask your municipality about the procedure when you enter workplace insurance. Check both sides of the change rather than assuming every procedure happens automatically. Route 2: voluntary continuation Voluntary continuation, 任意継続, lets eligible former members continue with their previous health insurer for a limited period. The following conditions are for Japan Health Insurance Association, also called Kyokai Kenpo. If you belonged to a health insurance society, 健康保険組合, ask that society for its own instructions. Do not treat this page as its application guide. For Kyokai Kenpo, you generally need at least two continuous months of insured membership up to your retirement date. Eligible Kyokai Kenpo applicants must submit the application to the responsible Kyokai Kenpo branch within 20 days, counted from the day after leaving employment. Postal applications must arrive by the deadline. If the twentieth day is a weekend or public holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day. Coverage can continue for up to two years, but it can end earlier under specified conditions. Ask about both application and termination procedures. You pay without the former employer's contribution. However, the premium is not always exactly twice your old deduction. Ask the insurer for an estimate and payment instructions. Route 3: National Health Insurance National Health Insurance, 国民健康保険, is arranged through your municipality. Ask whether you need to enrol when your workplace coverage ends. Act promptly. For example, Shinjuku City requires people who need to join its National Health Insurance to notify the city within 14 days of the event creating eligibility, such as losing workplace coverage. Confirm the relevant date, documents and submission method with your own municipality. Do not assume you have the same deadline as voluntary continuation. The amount depends on factors including previous income, household circumstances and the municipality's rules. Losing your salary does not necessarily make the first bill small. Ask for an estimate using your actual situation. If payment is difficult, ask whether any reduction or payment arrangement may apply. Do not assume a reduction is automatic. Route 4: a family member's workplace insurance You may qualify as a dependant, 被扶養者, under a family member's workplace health insurance. The insurer must check the conditions. Ask the family member's employer or insurer what income and household information is needed. Mention benefits or other income when asking. Do not assume that having no salary is enough. Wait for confirmation of eligibility and the start date. An application alone does not prove that coverage has begun. Health-insurance dependant status is not the same as pension Category III status. The pension route has separate conditions, including the relationship to the insured person. See the companion guide Pension when your work situation changes . Compare estimates, not guesses Collect estimates for the routes you are eligible to use. Ask each office what period its estimate covers and whether any part may change. A useful note might contain: The insurer or municipality's name. The proposed start date. The quoted premium and the period it covers. Any further documents needed. The application and payment deadlines. Your old payslip shows what was deducted while you were employed. It does not, on its own, show the cost after leaving. Use How to read your payslip if you need help finding the deduction. This guide does not identify a cheapest route. Compare confirmed estimates and eligibility before deciding. What to prepare Ask the receiving office for its current list. Depending on the procedure, useful information may include: Proof that your old insurance ended. Identity and My Number documents required by that office. The name of your former insurer. Information about income and household members. Details of any new workplace coverage. Documents accepted by one municipality or insurer may differ from another's. Do not send personal numbers or copies of private notices to this website. Foreign nationality alone does not decide which route applies. If you are also leaving Japan or changing your residence situation, ask the relevant office about those separate procedures. Useful words Japanese English meaning When you may use it 任意継続 Voluntary continuation When asking your former insurer about continuing coverage. 国民健康保険 National Health Insurance At your municipal insurance counter. 被扶養者 Dependant covered by another member When asking a family member's insurer about eligibility. 資格喪失証明書 Proof that insurance eligibility ended When requesting evidence from your former employer or insurer. 保険料 Insurance premium When asking how much you must pay. Related guides The companion guide I lost my job: what to do first covers the wider leaving-work checklist. Pension when your work situation changes covers the separate pension check. For medical visits, see Going to a clinic . If you are also moving, see Address registration . Official sources Kyokai Kenpo: voluntary continuation and post-employment options — the Kyokai Kenpo rules described here. Shinjuku City: National Health Insurance registration — one municipality's official instructions; check your own municipality too. Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare: health-insurance eligibility documents . Your former insurer, new employer and municipality remain the contacts for your own application.

title: Pension when your work situation changes
summary: Check pension registration after a work change, including a new employer, National Pension and support when payment is difficult.
keywords: Quick answer When a job ends, check what happens to your pension coverage. A new employer may enrol you in Employees' Pension Insurance. Otherwise, you may need a National Pension procedure, or a procedure through an eligible spouse's employer. If payment is difficult, ask about exemption or postponement. Do not assume unemployment makes registration or payments disappear automatically. First: check your current and next coverage Employees' Pension Insurance, 厚生年金, is pension coverage linked to eligible employment. National Pension, 国民年金, is the basic pension system. Start by asking your former employer when your Employees' Pension Insurance membership ends. If you have a new job, ask the new employer whether you will join and on what date. Do not assume that every job includes the same pension coverage. If there is a gap between jobs, ask the municipal pension counter or a pension office what procedure is needed. This guide explains where to start. It does not estimate your future pension or decide every person's eligibility. Which route should you check? Your situation What to check Who to ask Your new job includes Employees' Pension Insurance Enrolment and the start date Your new employer You live in Japan, are aged 20–59, and will not have Employees' Pension Insurance Whether you must register as a National Pension Category I member Your municipality or a pension office You may be supported by a spouse with eligible pension coverage Whether you qualify for National Pension Category III Your spouse's employer or a pension office You are outside the usual age range or have a special coverage situation The procedure for your circumstances A pension office Use the table to choose a contact, not to make a final eligibility decision yourself. Joining through a new employer Ask the new employer to confirm the pension start date. Tell the employer that you have an existing pension record. Keep your basic pension number information available. Ask which documents the employer needs. You should not need to work out the pension premium yourself to ask about enrolment. Your payslip can help you identify a pension deduction. If the deduction or coverage is unclear, ask payroll to explain it. Registering as a Category I member Category I, 第1号被保険者, is a National Pension membership category. It commonly applies to residents aged 20–59 who are not covered by Employees' Pension Insurance or as eligible dependent spouses. If you need to change to Category I after leaving work, submit the registration to your municipality within 14 days, counted from the day after leaving employment. Ask the pension counter if you are unsure whether this applies to you. Even a short gap between jobs can require a procedure. Do not skip the check because another job starts soon. Ask what to do if a document is missing. Tell the office your employment end date and which papers you are waiting for. Do not quietly leave the issue until a payment notice arrives. Checking Category III through a spouse Category III, 第3号被保険者, is a pension category for an eligible dependent spouse of a covered employee. It is not a category for every family member supported by someone else. Ask your spouse's employer whether you qualify and which procedure is needed. The employer handles the application route for eligible spouses. Health-insurance dependant status and pension Category III are different checks. For example, being a family member covered by health insurance does not, by itself, establish Category III pension eligibility. If the employee supporting a spouse leaves work, the spouse may also need to change pension registration. Ask about both people's records rather than checking only the person who left the job. What to prepare Check the office's current requirements. You may need: Your basic pension number document, or the My Number documents required for the procedure. Identity documents. Proof of the date your previous pension coverage ended, if requested. Information about the next employer or the spouse-based route you are checking. A pension number and a health-insurance membership number are not interchangeable. If you cannot find a document, ask the office how to proceed. Keep private numbers and document images out of messages to this website. Share them only through an appropriate official procedure. If paying is difficult Ask your municipality or pension office about an exemption, 免除, or payment postponement, 納付猶予. These require an application and review. They do not start automatically when you lose a job. Tell the office that your employment ended. A special unemployment rule may change how your previous income is considered. That does not mean every household qualifies: a spouse's or household head's income may still matter, depending on the application. Ask which evidence of unemployment is accepted. Separation documents or employment-insurance benefit documents may help support the application. If you receive partial exemption, a remaining premium may still need to be paid. Read the decision and ask how much to pay. Do not treat a partial exemption as a full exemption. An approved exemption or postponement is different from simply not paying. Ask the office how the decision affects your pension record. This guide does not calculate that effect or recommend a particular application for you. Notes for foreign residents Foreign residents can be subject to Japan's pension enrolment rules. Foreign nationality alone does not make registration unnecessary. If a social security agreement or another special arrangement may apply, ask a pension office. Bring information about the coverage you already have. This guide does not list all agreement exceptions. Leaving Japan involves a separate check. Do not assume that all pension contributions can be refunded. The Japan Pension Service has official departure guidance, including information about lump-sum withdrawal payments. Read that guidance before making a decision. Where to ask Former employer: the end date of workplace pension coverage. New employer: enrolment and the new coverage start date. Spouse's employer: a possible Category III procedure. Municipal pension counter: National Pension registration and exemption applications. Pension office: unclear coverage, special circumstances and pension-record questions. Ask about available language support before visiting. Write down your work dates and main question so the office can direct you to the right procedure. Useful words Japanese English meaning When you may use it 厚生年金 Employees' Pension Insurance When asking an employer about pension coverage. 国民年金 National Pension At a municipal pension counter. 第1号被保険者 Category I member When checking registration after leaving workplace coverage. 第3号被保険者 Category III member When checking the eligible dependent-spouse route. 免除 Premium exemption When asking about difficulty paying. 納付猶予 Payment postponement When asking whether an approved delay is available. 基礎年金番号 Basic pension number When finding or confirming your pension record. Related guides For the whole departure checklist, use the companion guide I lost my job: what to do first . For medical coverage, use Health insurance after leaving a job . See Take-home pay for the wider picture of salary deductions. See Health insurance for medical coverage basics. Official sources Japan Pension Service: employment and retirement procedures . Japan Pension Service: National Pension registration . Japan Pension Service: procedures after leaving work . Japan Pension Service: exemption and payment postponement . Japan Pension Service: National Pension enrolment in English . Japan Pension Service: leaving Japan .

title: Year-end Adjustment or a Tax Return in Japan?
summary: Does your employer handle your tax in Japan? Compare year-end adjustment and tax returns, including job changes, refunds and what to ask payroll.
keywords: Your employer has sent tax forms. Does completing them finish your tax paperwork, or do you also need to file a return? Start with the questions below.    Quick answer   For many employees, their employer uses  year-end adjustment (年末調整)  to settle income tax withheld from salary. A  tax return (確定申告)  is a separate procedure with the tax office. Some employees must file one; others may file to claim a refund. You can have year-end adjustment and still need a return.    Start with payroll  to check what your employer will handle.  Check with the tax office  if you have other income, an unadjusted job, or a deduction your employer cannot handle.    A simple decision guide      Are you receiving salary?  Ask payroll whether you qualify for year-end adjustment and which forms they need. If you are not an employee, check the tax-return rules for your income instead.    Will all relevant salary be included?  Mention any previous or second employer. Do not assume one employer handles every job.    Is anything outside the adjustment?  Other income, eligible medical expenses or a first-year housing-loan credit can require a separate check.    Still unsure?  Take your income records to the tax office. Ask whether filing is required or whether a refund claim may help. This guide is not an eligibility calculator.     Two ways to settle income tax       Question  Year-end adjustment  Tax return       Who handles it?  Your employer, using information you submit.  You file with the tax office, including through e-Tax.     When?  Usually at year-end. Follow your employer's forms deadline.  Normally in the following year; refund claims have different timing.     What does it cover?  Eligible salary income and deductions handled by payroll.  Income, deductions and tax credits reportable on your return.        What is year-end adjustment?   Tax taken from each salary payment is not necessarily your final annual tax. Your employer compares the amount withheld with the annual income tax, including the special income tax for reconstruction. The adjustment can mean a refund or additional tax.   Eligible employees generally submit the declaration for dependents to their employer. People employed throughout the year, or joining during the year and still employed at year-end, are typical cases. Exceptions and income limits apply. Ask payroll to confirm your eligibility.   For the deduction shown on your monthly statement, see  How to read your payslip .   What is a tax return?   A return reports the relevant income and deductions for January to December and settles tax after allowing for amounts already paid. It does not mean paying the same salary tax twice.   The usual filing period is  February 16 to March 15 of the following year , with calendar and special-case adjustments. For  2026 income, the usual filing season is in 2027 . Check the NTA's notice for that filing season before relying on a specific deadline.   e-Tax lets you submit a return electronically. The NTA's return-preparation service guides you through the figures. Check its current identity-verification and document requirements before starting.   When may year-end adjustment be enough?
